transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-09-05
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood SE), Aisha Rahman (Maple Health Lead Engineer), Tom Briggs (CTO), Marta Silva (Maple Health ML Eng)

Summary: quick sandbox onramp for Hosted API chat/text gen. Walkthrough of Console, Optimize suggestions, streaming behavior and retry/backoff patterns. Discussed latency vs cost tradeoffs, KV cache, batching, idempotency and enterprise questions (SOC2, VPC). Agreed next steps: sandbox invite, security docs, baseline perf pilot.

Topics: Console tour, Optimize recommendations, Streaming and SSE behavior, client retries and idempotency keys, cost controls (max tokens/stop sequences), demo curl + SDK, basic troubleshooting steps.

Action items (captured verbally): Jordan to share credits and pricing, Lena to run perf bench, Marta to share prompt set.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Jordan from Redwood, i'm joined by Lena from our SE team. how's that sound over there?
[00:06] Aisha: good, thanks for the invite. uh we've got a few minutes blocked to understand the sandbox and how streaming behaves, and the retry heuristics — and also Lina, sorry, Lena? yep.
[00:12] Lena: yep that's me. hi, excited to walk through — we'll try to keep it practical, demo the console, run a couple of API calls, and show Optimize's tuning tips.
[00:20] Tom: quick ask — we care about latency for conversational snippets, 200-400ms server to server ideally, and cost per 1k tokens is also a constraint.
[00:26] Jordan: totally, that's helpful. we'll show different knobs: model choices, batching, prefix cache (KV cache), and autoscaling behaviors that affect tail latency.
[00:34] Lena: if it's ok i'll share my screen — i'm going to open the Redwood Console sandbox. you should see a project called maple-health-sandbox if the invite landed.
[00:44] Marta: i actually haven't gotten the invite yet so maybe shout the link in the chat?
[00:47] Jordan: will do, sending link now. (typing) there it is.
[00:55] Lena: ok in the console home you can see run history and Optimize suggestions on the right, it's a lightweight set of recommended batching and quant profiles based on your sample traces. note: Optimize suggestions are heuristics from runtime telemetry, you can accept them or tweak.
[01:10] Aisha: the Optimize tab — what inputs does it use? sample prompts? traffic?
[01:14] Lena: mostly telemetry from actual inference runs — sequence length distribution, request concurrency, and failure patterns. it correlates cost per token and latency percentiles and recommends e.g. enable prefix KV cache for chat or reduce batch size for lower p99. it's not magic but it's a good starting point.
[01:30] Tom: curious about streaming — our front end relies on SSE chunks and needs partial tokens as soon as available. how deterministic is the stream ordering and what are backpressure behaviors?
[01:38] Lena: streaming uses chunked responses over server-sent events (SSE) or websockets. ordering is preserved per request. if the runtime sees load it may switch to smaller micro-batches which can increase throughput but can change inter-chunk timing, so you'll see more frequent smaller chunks. backpressure from your client is handled by connection-level flow control; we recommend an idle timeout of 60s and keep-alive heartbeats.
[02:00] Marta: and if a chunk fails mid-stream — do we retry from scratch or resume?
[02:04] Lena: by default the service is stateless per request so a mid-stream network failure requires a new request. to make retries cheap, we recommend using the streaming 'checkpoint' pattern: return partial responses and checkpoint text to your users, and when retrying, use the conversation history + the idempotency key so the server can apply prefix caching (KV cache) and skip repeated computation for earlier tokens. note that not all kernels support resuming from internal KV positions for different model variants — we'll point out which ones support cached resume.
[02:34] Jordan: to add, we provide an idempotency-key header and also an 'initial_cache_hint' you can set to ask the runtime to use the stored KV prefix if available. it's not a perfect resume but it can reduce duplicated compute.
[02:47] Aisha: is idempotency built into the SDK? we use typescript on the client side.
[02:51] Lena: yes, our JS SDK has automatic idempotency key generation for retries and exposes controls for maxRetries and backoffStrategy. example: sdk.chat.create({messages, idempotencyKey: 'auto', maxRetries:3}) — under the hood it adds exponential jittered backoff up to a configured max.
[03:08] Tom: ok that helps. can you show an example curl for streaming?
[03:12] Lena: sure — i'll run a quick curl:
[03:15] (sound of typing)
[03:17] Lena: curl -N -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Accept: text/event-stream" -d '{"model":"rwdomega-7b","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Summarize patient's recent visit in 2 bullets."}],"stream":true}' https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat/generate
[03:32] Marta: interesting — i see model rwdomega-7b there. what's the performance like for that vs say a quantized 7b?
[03:38] Lena: rwdomega is the default balanced model. quantized variants (q4 or q8) reduce memory and can slightly increase latency for small requests because indexing overhead changes, but reduce cost. Optimize will recommend quantization only when your throughput characteristics benefit. we'll share a quick matrix.
[03:55] Jordan: also worth mentioning caching: if your app frequently resumes conversations, prefix KV caching is usually the biggest win. we see 20-60% token CPU reduction depending on context length.
[04:05] Aisha: is there any induction-type behavior where cached prefixes cause wrong continuations?
[04:10] Lena: good callout — prefix caching replays the exact previous KV states, so it's deterministic for the same model and tokenizer config. if you change model versions, the cache is invalidated. for different model families results can diverge. also watch out for prompt engineering changes — if your system prompt changes frequently you may get unexpected outputs, so cache invalidation policy is important.
[04:30] Tom: what about timeouts and idempotency for long-running generations? we have some cases 2k+ tokens.
[04:36] Lena: for long gens we recommend chunked streaming with a lower per-chunk timeout and use explicit 'max_server_tokens' so the runtime can allocate buffer. for server-side timeouts set your client to 120s and have a waveform: short polling for chunk arrival and then fallback to a synchronous read for finalization. use idempotency keys to avoid duplicated writes if you persist the output in your DB.
[04:58] Marta: can we see Optimize suggestions for our sample traffic?
[05:02] Lena: i'll switch tabs — bring up the Optimize panel. it shows a recommendation to: reduce batch_size to 4 for p95 latency under 300ms, enable prefix cache for chat, and enable light quantization q8 for background tasks. it also suggests setting a token cap per-request to 1024 for cost control.
[05:18] Aisha: that token cap — will Optimize automatically truncate responses or will it error?
[05:22] Lena: it trims generation at the token cap; you can also configure a stop sequence. if you need partial outputs you should implement client-side continuation using the last message + cached prefix.
[05:34] Tom: security questions — SOC2 and network egress. we are heavily regulated, need SSO, audit logs, and possibly VPC peering or Private deployment.
[05:41] Jordan: we have SOC2 Type II, SAML SSO, RBAC in the console, and audit logs exported to your SIEM. For VPC, we offer a Private deployment option or VPC peering for Dedicated capacity — we'll share the network diagrams.
[05:58] Marta: if we do a Private deployment, does the same Console and Optimize experience remain?
[06:03] Jordan: yes, Private preserves the control plane features (console, optimize) but your inference nodes run in your VPC. there are some differences in telemetry retention for Optimize unless you enable ingestion to our control plane — we can discuss compliance-friendly telemetry flows.
[06:18] Aisha: excellent. i'm going to ask about the retry strategies again — what does Redwood recommend for client-side backoff constants?
[06:24] Lena: recommended default: exponential backoff starting at 200ms, multiplier 2, jitter 0.1-0.5, max attempts 3. for idempotent requests you can increase to 5. for streaming we recommend reconnect with a 'resumption' pattern: if connection lost within first 2 seconds, immediate retry, otherwise wait exponential.
[06:46] Marta: any guidance on concurrency when using Dedicated vs Hosted? our load profile is bursty e.g. spikes at 200 concurrent small chats.
[06:53] Jordan: Dedicated capacity gives you guaranteed GPU pools and predictable throughput; hosted is multi-tenant with soft quota and autoscaling. for bursty loads Dedicated with autoscale buffer is generally cheaper at scale because you avoid eviction latencies; Optimize can suggest pooling and batching settings to smooth spikes.
[07:10] Tom: can you show a quick SDK snippet for Typescript that demonstrates streaming and graceful reconnect?
[07:15] Lena: sure — (paraphrased) const stream = sdk.chat.stream({messages, onDelta: (d)=> render(d), idempotencyKey:'auto', retryOptions:{maxRetries:3, backoffMs:200}}); stream.on('error', (e)=> { /* reconnect logic using idempotency key */ })
[07:33] Aisha: will the server return a unique request id so we can tie logs?
[07:36] Lena: yes every response has x-request-id header and we emit trace ids to the console trace view. you can click into a request and see p50/p95/tokens/cost.
[07:46] Jordan: quick live test — Lena, can you generate a short doc summary and demonstrate a transient network failure retry?
[07:52] Lena: yep i'll send a sample request and then drop the connection from my side — simulate a client failure to show retry semantics.
[08:00] (typing, short pause)
[08:05] Lena: starting generation... stream chunk 1 arrives "Patient reported mild chest pain..." — now i'll cut network (simulated).
[08:15] (static)
[08:18] Lena: reconnecting with same idempotency key... new request hits runtime, Optimize saw same prefix, used KV cache and resumed effectively; second run returned final two bullets quickly, we avoided full recompute.
[08:33] Marta: awesome, that was helpful.
[08:36] Aisha: small nit — if we have PII, how's data handled in hosted mode? retention windows?
[08:41] Jordan: hosted retains logs for 30 days by default; you can request shorter retention or opt out of telemetry for specific orgs. for PHI workloads we recommend Private deployment or Dedicated with VPC + customer-managed KMS. we can share a PSR (privacy and security) doc.
[08:58] Tom: can you send the checklist for HIPAA-like compliance?
[09:02] Jordan: yes will include in the follow-up.
[09:05] Lena: another operational note: batching improves GPU utilization but can add tail latency — Optimize will show simulated p50/p95 change if you toggle batch size. generally small chats (few tokens) use batch size 1-4 to keep p95 low; background batch jobs use larger batch sizes for cost efficiency.
[09:25] Marta: what's the typical overhead if we enable prefix caching? any cold start penalty?
[09:29] Lena: cold start penalty is roughly ~10-30ms depending on model size; warm cached prefixes reduce forward compute and save up to 60% token compute for long contexts. cache hit rates depend on your conversation similarity.
[09:45] Aisha: are there per-route quotas or token limits we should be aware of?
[09:50] Jordan: yes you can set per-route quotas and per-token caps in the console, and configure per-team rate limits. we'll include an example policy JSON in the follow-up.
[09:59] Tom: any gotchas with tokenization differences across models? our prompts are medically heavy with special tokens sometimes.
[10:05] Lena: tokenization can differ across families; we recommend normalizing whitespace and using the same tokenizer when comparing token counts. Optimize reports token distribution by model so you can pick the most efficient variant.
[10:18] Marta: about cost — does Optimize give us an estimate of monthly spend for a given traffic profile?
[10:22] Lena: yes there's a cost estimator: input your expected rps, avg tokens in/out, and it projects monthly spend across model variants and recommends cheaper model families for background summarization.
[10:32] Aisha: let's talk about observability — can we get per-customer tracing over time and structured logs?
[10:37] Jordan: console has per-request traces, and audit logs can be pushed to your logging endpoint (S3 or SIEM). we also provide token-level cost breakdown per request in the trace view.
[10:48] Tom: what about safety filters — we need a sanity layer to avoid hallucinations when summarizing clinical notes.
[10:53] Lena: you can add post-generation reranks or structured output validators with function-calling style responses. Optimize can run evals on a held-out prompt set and detect quality regressions, we also support rule-based filters.
[11:07] Marta: can evals be integrated into CI?
[11:09] Lena: yes the eval API can be triggered from CI, it runs your prompt set against a model and returns diff metrics — you can gate rollouts on those metrics.
[11:18] Aisha: great. i'm timing us — we have about 30 minutes left, maybe move to ramp plan and next steps?
[11:24] Jordan: sure. proposed ramp: 1) sandbox creds and 30 credits, 2) Redwood runs baseline perf tests with your prompt set (Lena), 3) 1-week pilot on Hosted with Optimize turned on, 4) check security requirements and evaluate Dedicated/Private if needed.
[11:37] Tom: sounds good. Marta and Aisha will produce a short acceptance criteria doc.
[11:41] Marta: will do.
[11:43] Aisha: can we also get a checklist for instrumentation (headers to send, idempotency key, trace id)?
[11:48] Lena: yes, I'll paste a small 'instrumentation checklist' in the follow-up. it includes x-request-id, idempotency-key, user-id, and session metadata.
[11:58] Jordan: any other questions?
[12:00] Tom: one last one — concurrency limits on free sandbox?
[12:03] Jordan: sandbox has a soft quota of 10 rps and 4 concurrent streams; for the pilot we'll raise that to mirror your expected load.
[12:12] Aisha: thanks, that helps.
[12:15] Jordan: ok we'll wrap — i'll summarize and send notes + links to the recording and docs.
[12:22] Lena: action items: i'll run the baseline perf and attach traces; Jordan will share security docs and credits. Marta will share prompts.
[12:33] Tom: thanks all, look forward to the pilot.
[12:36] Jordan: thanks everyone. bye.

(End of transcript)
